title: Running Local Open-Weight LLMs (LM Studio / Ollama): GGUF VRAM Math & Checkpoint Caching
summary: Break free from cloud API bills and data-privacy concerns. Build a zero-dependency OpenAI-Compatible local client with GGUF VRAM budgeting, <think> block stripping, SHA-256 checkpoint caching, and single-GPU batch scheduling.
aeo_capsule: Local Open-Weight LLM Engineering pairs estimate_gguf_vram_gb memory budgeting, clean_local_llm_output reasoning-tag scrubbing, and CachedLocalLlmClient SHA-256 checkpoint caching with an injectable transport layer for deterministic, zero-bill single-GPU pipelines.
learning_objectives: Estimate total GGUF VRAM across model weights, linear KV Cache growth, and runtime overhead to prevent single-GPU OOM crashes
Build a zero-dependency OpenAI-Compatible client for LM Studio and Ollama with an injectable transport for offline CI unit testing
Combine reasoning_effort control, <think> tag scrubbing, and SHA-256 checkpoint caching for resumable single-GPU batch workflows

sections.heading: 8.1 GGUF Quantization and the Three-Part VRAM Budget
paragraphs: When engineers deploy their first local open-weight LLM, they often glance at the GGUF file size on disk and assume a 12 GB or 16 GB GPU has plenty of headroom. The moment they open a long conversation window, the runtime either throws an Out-of-Memory (OOM) error or silently spills layers into system RAM, slashing throughput from 40 tokens/sec down to single digits. Whether a model truly fits on a single card depends on three components combined: static weights, KV Cache, and runtime overhead. In examples/ai_ch08_local_llm_client.py, estimate_gguf_vram_gb formalizes this budget cleanly: weights_gb = params_billion * (quant_bits / 8.0), kv_cache_gb = (context_k / 8.0) * (params_billion * 0.04), plus 1.2 GB of fixed CUDA context and activation overhead.

Plugging our runnable benchmark—a 26B model quantized at Q4_K_M (roughly 4.5 effective bits per weight) with an 8k context window—gives 14.625 GB for weights, 1.04 GB for KV Cache, and 1.2 GB for runtime overhead, totaling 16.865 GB (rounded to 16.86 GB under Python's banker's rounding). Notice why we model Q4_K_M at 4.5 bits rather than a flat 4.0 bits: llama.cpp's K-Quants mixed quantization preserves higher precision (such as Q6_K) on sensitive attention and output tensors while compressing less sensitive weights aggressively, cutting footprint by over 70% versus FP16 without wrecking reasoning stability.

The most frequent hidden trap in local inference is oversizing context_k. Cranking LM Studio or Ollama up to 64k or 128k context by default causes KV Cache allocations to grow linearly, easily adding several gigabytes on 26B-32B models and pushing weights off the GPU. For batch summarization, translation, and structured extraction jobs, keeping context in the 4K-8K sweet spot and reserving 1.5-2.0 GB of free VRAM headroom keeps single-GPU runs fast and crash-free for hours.
bullets: Three-part VRAM formula: static weights (params * quant_bits / 8) + linear KV Cache growth + ~1.2 GB runtime overhead
A 26B Q4_K_M (4.5-bit) model at 8k context budgets to 16.86 GB; inflating context to 32k+ sharply raises OOM risk
Q4_K_M mixed quantization protects high-impact layers, saving ~72% VRAM while preserving code and JSON accuracy
sections.callout_title: Engineering Note: Batch Multi-Model Pipelines by Stage on a Single GPU
sections.callout_body: If you run a dual-model workflow (such as one model for drafting and another for polishing) on a single consumer GPU, never swap models back and forth per paragraph—cold-loading 15-20 GB of weights from SSD costs 15-20 seconds every switch. Run all Stage 1 chunks on Model A first, unload VRAM cleanly with lms unload --all, then load Model B once for Stage 2.

sections.heading: 8.2 Zero-Dependency OpenAI-Compatible Client & <think> Scrubbing
paragraphs: Modern local inference servers—whether LM Studio (default port 1234, favored for GUI inspection and lms CLI scheduling) or Ollama (default port 11434, favored for container and daemon deployments)—expose standard OpenAI-Compatible Chat Completions endpoints (/v1/chat/completions). Your application code does not need heavy vendor SDKs: assembling a plain JSON payload with model, temperature, max_tokens, and messages lets you swap local and cloud backends seamlessly. CachedLocalLlmClient goes one step further by injecting the transport layer as a Callable[[dict, ...], dict], completely decoupling orchestration logic from urllib or httpx.

Dependency-injected transport pays off immediately in two ways. First, in GPU-less CI environments like GitHub Actions, unit tests pass an in-memory mock_lm_studio callable and validate payload assembly, tag stripping, and caching in milliseconds with zero network calls. Second, upgrading production transport with custom timeouts, exponential backoff, or async HTTP pooling requires swapping one callable without touching cache keys or cleaning logic.

Modern reasoning-capable open models (such as Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1, or Gemma variants) introduce two classic output hazards: inline <think>...</think> chain-of-thought blocks emitted before the answer, and outer ```json ... ``` Markdown code fences even when instructed to emit raw JSON. Passing raw output straight into json.loads() crashes downstream parsers. Our client mitigates both simultaneously: it sets reasoning_effort: none and low temperature (0.2) in the payload to suppress unnecessary thinking tokens, and passes raw content through clean_local_llm_output—applying THINK_BLOCK_RE (with re.DOTALL | re.IGNORECASE) followed by FENCE_RE to recover clean {"status": "ready"} JSON.
bullets: LM Studio (port 1234) and Ollama (port 11434) share OpenAI-Compatible APIs; injecting transport enables 100% offline CI unit tests
Set reasoning_effort to none and low temperature (0.2) on deterministic extraction or translation tasks to eliminate wasted thinking tokens
clean_local_llm_output strips multiline <think> blocks and outer Markdown fences before downstream JSON parsing
sections.callout_title: Security Baseline: Bind Local Inference Servers Strictly to 127.0.0.1
sections.callout_body: Keep LM Studio Server and Ollama bound strictly to 127.0.0.1 (localhost) unless placed behind an authenticated reverse proxy on a private network. Local inference servers ship without authentication by default; exposing 0.0.0.0 invites unauthorized LAN or internet hosts to hijack your GPU and inspect active sessions.

sections.heading: 8.3 SHA-256 Content-Addressed Checkpoint Caching
paragraphs: Batch-processing dozens of book chapters or thousands of records on a single local GPU can run for 30 to 60 minutes. Without checkpoint caching, a single malformed JSON response, driver reset, or power blip forces you to recompute every completed chunk from scratch. CachedLocalLlmClient implements classic content-addressed caching with zero external dependencies: _cache_key serializes [self.model_id, system_prompt, user_prompt] into deterministic JSON and hashes it with hashlib.sha256, slicing the first 16 hex characters as a compact cache key.

Including all three elements—model_id, system_prompt, and user_prompt—inside the hash is critical for correctness. Whenever you upgrade from one local model to another or tighten a glossary rule in the system prompt, the computed SHA-256 key changes automatically and triggers fresh inference, preventing silent stale-cache contamination. Conversely, our live run sends the exact same Ping status prompt twice and confirms the second call serves directly from self.cache with self.api_calls remaining at 1.

Promoting the in-memory dictionary self.cache into a crash-resilient production batch runner requires only one extra step: atomic disk persistence. Write each validated chunk to a temporary file inside .forge_cache/ and commit via os.replace (or store rows in SQLite). If step 8 of a 10-step pipeline fails or you refine post-processing code, rerunning the script replays steps 1 through 7 from disk in milliseconds and resumes GPU inference immediately at step 8.
bullets: Hash model_id, system_prompt, and user_prompt together with SHA-256 so model swaps or prompt edits automatically invalidate stale entries
Identical repeated prompts hit cache before calling transport (api_calls stays 1 in live verification), eliminating redundant GPU work
Persist validated outputs atomically to disk JSON files or SQLite so long batch pipelines resume cleanly after any interruption
sections.callout_title: Refinement: Hash Inference Hyperparameters Too When They Vary
sections.callout_body: If your pipeline varies temperature, max_tokens, or JSON Schema constraints dynamically for the same model and prompt, include those parameters in _cache_key as well—while stripping purely diagnostic timestamps before hashing so cache hit rates remain high.

sections.heading: 8.4 Local Production Best Practices: Resilience, Validation & VRAM Cleanup
paragraphs: Turning a local model into a dependable production worker requires three operational safeguards beyond VRAM math and caching. First, enforce an output contract gate before caching: even with reasoning disabled and clean_local_llm_output applied, smaller quantized models can still truncate JSON at max_tokens or emit unescaped quotes. Pair the client with Chapter 2's structured validation retry loop (2-3 attempts feeding parse errors back to the model) and write to the checkpoint cache only after validation passes so corrupted artifacts are never persisted.

Second, separate lightweight health checks from inference timeouts. Cold-loading a large GGUF file or prefilling a long prompt can easily take 15-30 seconds before the first token arrives, tripping default 5-second web timeouts. Probe server readiness cheaply with GET /v1/models (LM Studio) or GET /api/tags (Ollama) before starting a batch, then configure generous read timeouts (180-300 seconds) with exponential backoff on /v1/chat/completions to ride out transient connection refusals during startup.

Third, automate VRAM teardown. Leaving a 16-20 GB model resident on a desktop GPU after a batch script finishes starves browsers, editors, and subsequent jobs of video memory. Wrap every batch runner in a Python try...finally block that explicitly unloads models on exit (such as lms unload --all or Ollama keep_alive: 0). With accurate VRAM budgeting, injected offline tests, output scrubbing, checkpoint caching, and clean teardown, a single workstation GPU becomes a zero-marginal-cost, privacy-preserving AI factory.
bullets: Validate before caching: only persist cleaned outputs after JSON Schema or linter checks pass to keep checkpoints pristine
Use GET /v1/models or /api/tags for zero-compute health probes and set generous read timeouts for long prompt prefill
Always unload GPU models inside try...finally blocks so workstation VRAM is returned cleanly on both success and failure
sections.callout_title: Pre-Flight Checklist for Single-GPU Batch Pipelines
sections.callout_body: Before starting a long batch run: (1) verify total VRAM with estimate_gguf_vram_gb leaving >= 1.5 GB headroom, (2) confirm the server listens only on 127.0.0.1, (3) run offline unit tests with mock_lm_studio to verify <think> stripping and cache hits, and (4) ensure finally-block teardown unloads VRAM.

pitfalls.title: Pitfall 1: Oversizing Context Windows Until KV Cache Triggers OOM
pitfalls.symptom: Model weights look smaller than your GPU capacity, yet loading with 64k or 128k context causes immediate OOM crashes or silent CPU RAM spilling that cuts speed by 10x.
pitfalls.root_cause_and_fix: KV Cache grows linearly with context length. Run estimate_gguf_vram_gb before loading, keep batch jobs inside the 4K-8K golden window, and preserve at least 1.5-2.0 GB of free VRAM headroom.

pitfalls.title: Pitfall 2: Leaving <think> Blocks or Markdown Fences Unscrubbed Before JSON Parsing
pitfalls.symptom: Reasoning-capable open models prepend multiline <think>...</think> blocks or wrap answers in ```json ... ``` fences, causing json.loads() to raise JSONDecodeError.
pitfalls.root_cause_and_fix: Pass reasoning_effort: none for formatting/extraction tasks and always scrub raw responses through clean_local_llm_output() before parsing—and only write validated results into your checkpoint cache.

pitfalls.title: Pitfall 3: Exposing Unauthenticated Local Ports or Forgetting VRAM Teardown
pitfalls.symptom: Binding LM Studio or Ollama to 0.0.0.0 opens free GPU access to the LAN; or leaving a 20 GB model loaded after a script ends starves desktop apps and subsequent jobs.
pitfalls.root_cause_and_fix: Bind local inference endpoints strictly to 127.0.0.1 unless fronted by an authenticated proxy, and wrap batch scripts in try...finally blocks that run lms unload --all or release VRAM automatically.

quiz.question: Using estimate_gguf_vram_gb(params_billion, quant_bits=4.5, context_k=8), what is the estimated total VRAM for an 8B Q4_K_M (4.5-bit) model at 8k context (including KV Cache and 1.2 GB overhead)?
quiz.explanation: Weights = 8.0 * (4.5 / 8.0) = 4.50 GB, KV Cache = (8 / 8) * (8.0 * 0.04) = 0.32 GB, and runtime overhead = 1.20 GB, giving a total of 6.02 GB.

quiz.question: In CachedLocalLlmClient._cache_key(), why must self.model_id and system_prompt be hashed alongside user_prompt?
options: Because Python's hashlib.sha256 requires at least three input elements
So upgrading models or editing system instructions automatically invalidates stale cached responses instead of serving outdated answers
To compress the GPU's internal KV Cache memory footprint
Because OpenAI-Compatible APIs reject repeated user_prompt strings
quiz.explanation: This cache stores application-level text completions. Omitting model_id or system_prompt from the SHA-256 key would return stale completions from an older model or prompt after configuration changes.

quiz.question: Why must THINK_BLOCK_RE in clean_local_llm_output() enable the re.DOTALL flag?
options: So the dot (.) wildcard matches newline characters and removes multiline <think>...</think> reasoning blocks completely
To anchor matching strictly to the start of the string
To convert cleaned strings directly into Python dicts
quiz.explanation: By default, regex '.' does not match newline characters (\n). Because chain-of-thought <think> blocks almost always span multiple lines, omitting re.DOTALL leaves the entire reasoning block intact.

interview_faqs.question: How do LM Studio and Ollama differ in engineering workflows, and when should you pick each?
interview_faqs.answer: Both wrap llama.cpp with OpenAI-Compatible APIs, but optimize for different ergonomics. LM Studio (port 1234) shines on developer workstations with visual model inspection, fine-grained GPU offload controls, and the lms CLI for scripted single-GPU load/unload staging. Ollama (port 11434) excels as a lightweight background daemon with Modelfiles, making it straightforward to deploy inside Docker containers or systemd services.

interview_faqs.question: Does Q4_K_M quantization hurt code generation or structured JSON reliability?
interview_faqs.answer: For modern 14B-35B open models, Q4_K_M (~4.5 bits/weight) hits the practical sweet spot: it saves over 70% VRAM relative to FP16 while protecting sensitive attention layers via K-Quants mixed precision, causing only minor perplexity drift. For smaller 7B-8B models under strict JSON Schema constraints, stepping up to Q6_K or Q8_0—paired with schema retry loops—further improves structural compliance.

interview_faqs.question: How do you run a zero-compute health check against a local LLM server?
interview_faqs.answer: Never probe health via /v1/chat/completions, which triggers real GPU prefill and decode work. Instead, send a lightweight GET to http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1/models on LM Studio or GET http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/tags (and /api/ps for loaded models) on Ollama to verify HTTP 200 readiness with negligible overhead.

interview_faqs.question: How do you prevent dynamic fields like timestamps or request IDs from breaking SHA-256 cache hits?
interview_faqs.answer: Keep non-semantic telemetry such as request_id and timestamps out of the prompt body—pass them via HTTP headers or external logs instead. When prompts legitimately contain dynamic metadata, normalize or separate volatile fields before computing _cache_key so expensive static document processing still achieves high cache hit rates.
